la:adj:maritimus.gloss: Of or pertaining to the sea; marine, maritime.
senses: Of or pertaining to the sea; marine, maritime.
la:adj:maritimus.html:
mărĭtĭmus (mărĭtŭmus), a, um, adj.
mare
,
of or belonging to the sea, sea-, maritime (class.).
Lit.: fluctus movi maritumos,: homines maritimi,seamen, mariners,; cf. absol.: e barbaris ipsis nulli erant antea maritimi praeter Etruscos et Poenos,: maritimus et navalis hostis,: loci maritimi, an remoti a mari,: urbes,on the seacoast, lying on the sea,; : civitas,: portus,: agri,: provincia,: ora,; : cursus,a voyage,: res,maritime affairs,: naves,sea-going,: officium,: ecfugere a vita marituma,: bellum,with the pirates,: portus, navibus ab maritima vi tutus,: sal,sea-salt,: silvae,on the sea-coast,: nuptiae, i. e. those of Peleus with Thetis (opp. terrenae nuptiae, i. e. with Musa), : usurae,from maritime speculations,.—Subst.: mărĭtĭma, ōrum, n., maritime parts or places: in maritimis sum,; so with gen.: maritima Aetoliae vastare,: maritima Africae,: Tarraconis,.—*
Transf., changeable, inconstant, like the sea: mores,.

la:noun:mare.html:
măre, is (
abl. sing. mare, Varr. ap. and 111 P.; and in ib.; ; ; ; ; ; gen. plur. marum, Naev. ap. P.), n.
root mar-, gleam, glimmer (cf. ἅλς μαρμαρέη, Il. 14, 273); Gr. μάρμαρος; Lat. marmor; Sanscr. mīras, sea; Goth. marei; Angl. - Sax. mere; Germ. Meer. Curtius, however, refers these words to root mar-, die; cf. morior, marceo
, the sea, opp. to dry land.
Lit.
In gen.: sol, qui Mare, terram, caelum contines tuo cum lumine, Enn. ap. Prob. (Trag. v. 322 Vahl.): indu mari magno, id. ap. (Ann. v. 425 ib.): mare infidum,: fluctuosum,: ventosum,: tumultuosum,: tumidum,: placidum,: tranquillum,: vastissimum,: vastum atque apertum,: profundum et immensum,: planum,: numquam ingressus es mare,: mare pedibus ingredi,: remenso ire mari,: terrā marique, by sea and by land: terra marique acquirenda,i. e. at all hazards,; v. terra.—In plur.: maria salsa, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 145 Vahl.): quibus cavernis maria sustineantur,: in reliquis maribus,.—Poet. as a figure for hard-heartedness: te saevae progenuere ferae Aut mare, etc.,; cf. ; cf. also: Nam mare haud est mare; vos mare acerrumum; nam in mari repperi, hic elavi bonis,: meretricem ego item esse reor mare ut est; quod des devorat, numquam abundat,—In apposition with Oceanus: proximus mare Oceanum in Andibus hiemarat,; ; cf. also: ecce maris magna claudit nos obice pontus,the depths of the sea,: maria omnia caelo Miscere,.—Prov.: mare caelo miscere, to mingle sea and sky, i. e. to raise a terrific storm, bluster: clames licet, et mare caelo Confundas, homo sum,: quis caelum terris non misceat et mare caelo,: terrā marique aliquid quaerere or conquirere, to search for a thing by sea and land, i. e. everywhere, ; Vatin. ap. ; : maria et montes polliceri, to promise seas and mountains, i. e. more than one can perform, : his qui contentus non est, in mare fundat aquas, pour water into the sea, i. e. fill that which is already full, .—
In partic., of single seas: mare nostrum,i. e. the Mediterranean Sea,; ; ; : mare superum,the Upper Sea, the Adriatic,; ; ; ; : mare inferum, the Etruscan Sea, Cic. l. l.; ; Mel. l. l.; Plin. l. l. al.: mare Aegeum,: mare rubrum, v. ruber; of a fresh - water lake: Galileae,.—
Transf. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Sea-water, salt-water: Chium maris expers,unmixed Chian wine, (id est, sine aqua marina, Schol. Acr.); so, vinum mari condire,.—
The color of the sea, sea-green: smaragdi virens mare,. —*
Of the air: mare aëris, the sea, i. e. expanse of air: id omne Aëris in magnum fertur mare,.—
A large vessel: bases et mare aëneum,.

la:other:Marius.html:
Mărĭus, i, m.,
the name of a Roman gens.
The most celebrated is C. Marius, the conqueror of Jugurtha, and seven times consul, ; ; ; sqq.; as a friend of the popular party, his name is used as an appellative: Caesari multos Marios inesse, Cæsar had many Mariuses in him, Sulla ap. —
M. Marius Gratidianus, ; ; ; ; Sen. de Ira, 3, 18; .—
Marius Priscus, proconsul in Africa, tried for extortion, A. D. 100, ; ; . —
Marius Victorinus, a rhetorician and grammarian, a native of Africa, in the middle of the fourth century of the Christian era. —Hence,
Mărĭus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to C. Marius, Marian: lex,.—
Mărĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to C. Marius, Marian: Mariani consulatus,: scutum Cimbricum,: quercus,: tribunus plebis,: Mariana et Sullana tempestas,: Mariana et Cinnana rabies,.—Subst.: Mărĭāna, ae, f., a Roman colony on the eastern coast of Corsica, founded by C. Marius, ; .—Plur. subst.: Mărĭ-āni, ōrum, m., another name of the Cernetari in Latium, .

la:noun:Mars.html:
Mars (archaic and poet. Māvors, q. v.), Martis (collat. reduplic. form Marmar, in the Song of the Arval Brothers; v. the following, and Mamers), m.
root mar-, gleam; Sanscr. marīkis, beam of light; hence Mars, the bright god; cf.: marmor, mare
,
Mars, who, as father of Romulus, was the primogenitor of the Roman people, the god of war, of husbandry, of shepherds and seers. For him was named the month of Martius, March, the beginning of the Roman year, sqq.: legio Martia ... ab eo deo, a quo populum Romanum generatum accepimus,: Mars pater te precor quaesoque, uti sies volens propitius mihi, etc., ... ut tu morbos visos invisosque viduertatem vastitudinemque, calamitates intemperiasque prohibessis, etc.,; cf., in the Song of the Arval Brothers, NEVE LVERVE MARMAR SINS INCVRRERE IN PLEORIS; for Mars pater, the forms Marspiter, gen. Marspitris, or -tĕris, and Maspiter were also employed,; ; ; Müll.; 9, § 75; 10, § 65; : Mars Gradivus, Quirinus, Silvanus, Ultor, v. under h. vv.: Mars durus,: torvus,: cruentus,: ferus,; : ferox,: bellicus,: fortibus sane oculis Cassius (Martem spirare dicens) se in Siciliam non iturum,. The Salii were destined for his service, ; horses and bulls were offered to him, Paul. ex Müll.; ; : per Martem, a soldier's oath,. He was often appealed to in oaths, etc., esp. by soldiers: Nam neque Duellona mi umquam neque Mars creduat, ni, etc.,; ; .—
Transf.
War, battle, a conflict, engagement, contest, etc.; also the art of war: cum veter occubuit Priamus sub Marte Pelasgo, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 17 Vahl.): Martem accendere cantu,to incite to battle,: apertus,fighting in the open field,: equitem suo alienoque Marte pugnare, i. e. to fight both in their own fashion (on horseback) and in one which was strange to them (on foot), : pugna jam in manus, jam in gladios, ubi Mars est atrocissimus, venerat,: terribili Marte ululare,: captam sine Marte,: quos amisimus cives, eos Martis vis perculit, non ira victoriae,.—Poet.: Mars forensis,a contest in the forum, legal contest,; cf.: et fora Marte suo litigiosa vacent,.—Hence, prov.: suo (nostro, vestro) Marte, by one's own exertions, without the assistance of others: rex ipse suo Marte res suas recuperavit,; : cum vos vestro Marte his rebus omnibus abundetis,.—
The issue of a war or a battle, the fortune of war: cum omnis belli Mars communis, et cum semper incerti exitus proeliorum sint,: communis adhuc Mars belli erat, : aequo Marte,with equal advantage, on equal terms,; ; : pari Marte,: aequato Marte,: verso Marte ( = versā fortunā),: vario Marte pugnatum est,: incerto Marte,: anceps,; : dubius,.—
The planet Mars: Jovis stellae proximum inferiorem orbem tenet πυρόεις, quae stella Martis appellatur, ; ; ; ; : Martis sidus,.—Hence,
Mar-tĭus (Māvortĭus, v.infra), a, um, adj.
Of or belonging to Mars: lupus,sacred to Mars,; cf.: Martius lupus, integer et intactus, gentis nos Martiae et conditoris nostri admonuit, descended from Mars (since Mars is the father of Romulus and Remus), : legio,; : miles,: proles,i. e. Romulus and Remus,: anguis,sacred to Mars,: judicium,i. e. of the Areopagus at Athens, Oud.: Campus; v. campus: harena,a place in the Circus where the gladiators fought,; : gramen,i. e. the Field of Mars,: Martius mensis, the month of March, formerly the first month of the year, : Martii Calendis,: Idus Martiae, the Ides of March, famous as the day on which Julius Cæsar was killed, ; cf. 14, 20, 1 sq.; ; .— In the form Mavortius (poet.): moenia,i. e. Rome,: tellus,i. e. Thrace,: conjux,i. e. Venus,: proles,i. e. the Thebans,; cf.: seges belli (because sprung from the dragon's teeth),.—
Transf.
Warlike, martial: Martia Penthesilea,: Martia saeculi voluptas,: Martius aeris rauci canor,: vulnera,: Thebe,i. e. where many wars were carried on,.—
Of or belonging to the planet Mars: ille fulgor rutilus, horribilisque terris, quem Martium dicitis,.—As subst.: Mar-tĭus, ii, m. (sc. mensis), March, the month of March: Mensium nomina fere aperta sunt, si a Martio, ut antiqui constituerunt, numeres, Nam primus a Marte,.—
Martĭālis, e, adj.
Of or belonging to Mars: Flamen, Varr L. L. 5, § 84 Müll.; 7, § 45 ib.: lupus,sacred to Mars,: ludi,in honor of Mars,: Martialis collis, near the temple of Deus Fidius, Müll.—Subst.: Martĭālis, is, m., a priest of Mars: Martiales quidam Larini appellabantur, ministri publici Martis,.—
Belonging to the legio Martia; hence, Martĭāles, the soldiers of the legio Martia, .

Marcellĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Marcellus, Marcellian: theatrum, named after M. Claudius Marcellus, the nephew of Augustus, ; .

la:adj:maritus.html:
mărītus, a, um, adj.
mas
,
of or belonging to marriage, matrimonial, conjugal, nuptial, marriage-.
Adj. (so mostly poet.; not in Cic.).
Lit.: facibus cessit maritis,to the nuptial torches, to wedlock,faces,: foedus,the conjugal tie,: tori,: sacra, (4, 20, 16); : Venus,wedded love,; cf.: fides,conjugal fidelity, lex, respecting marriage, a marriage-law (de maritandis ordinibus, ), .—In prose: vagabatur per maritas domos dies noctesque,i. e. the houses of married people, Drak.—
Transf.
Of plants, wedded, i. e. tied up (cf. marito, II. B.): arbores,; : ulmo conjuncta marito (sc. vitis),; : olivetum,.—
Impregnating, fertilizing (in postclass. poetry): fluctus (Nili),: imbres, Pervigil. Ven. 4, 11.—
Subst.
mărītus, i, m., a married man, husband (freq. and class.; cf. conjux, vir): ditis damnosos maritos sub basilica quaerito,: ut maritus sis quam optimae (mulieris),: sororis,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Val Max. 8, 2, 14; et saep.: insidian

iem somno maritorum, : quae major calumnia est quam venire imberbum adulescentem, bene valentem ac maritum,; ; opp. coelebs: seu maritum sive coelibem scortarier,; ; ; ; : bonus optandusque maritus,: malus ingratusque maritus,: mariti testamentum,: patrius,: Phrygio servire marito,: unico gaudens mulier marito,: novus,a newly-married man, a young husband,: intra quartum et vicesimum annum maritus,: recens,: ut juveni primum virgo deducta marito,: lex Bithynorum, si quid mulier contrahat, maritum auctorem esse jubet,: si maritus pro muliere se obligaverit,: maritus lugendus decem mensibus,.—

Transf.
A lover, suitor (poet.), (3, 14), 10: aegram (Dido) nulli quondam flexere mariti,.—
Of animals: ol ens maritus,i. e. a he-goat,: quem pecori dixere maritum,; so, gregum,; of cocks,; .—
In plur.: mă-rīti, ōrum, m., married people, man and wife (post-class.), : novi mariti,newly-married people, a young couple,.—
mărīta, ae, f., a married woman, wife (poet. and postclass.): marita,: castae maritae,; ; ; ; and freq. on epitaphs.

la:verb:marito.gloss: to marry, wed (in the sense of "give a husband to someone", "give someone in marriage")
senses: to marry, wed (in the sense of "give a husband to someone", "give someone in marriage")
to be coupled; to have a mate
la:verb:marito.html:
mărīto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
1. maritus
,
to give a husband to one; hence to wed, marry, give in marriage to a man.
Lit. (post-Aug. and rare): Vitellii filiam,: lex (Augusti) de maritandis ordinibus,i. e. imposing fines for celibacy in all classes,: lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus,; ; pleonastically: matrimonia,i. e. to conclude, make,.—Hence, absol., to marry, take a wife: maritandum principem suaderent,.—
Transf.
Of animals and plants.
Pass.: maritari, to be coupled, i. e. to have a mate: tunc dicuntur catulire, id est ostendere, se velle maritari,.—
To impregnate: (Zephyrus) glebas fecundo rore maritat,; so in pass., to be impregnated: quae (feminae) ternae singulis (maribus) maritantur,; ; .—
Of plants, to wed, i. e. to tie or fasten to another tree: adultā vitium propagine Altas maritat populos,: ulmi vitibus maritantur,; : maritandae arbores,; cf. .—Hence, mărītātus, a, um, P. a., of or pertaining to a wife.—Comic.: A. Pulchra dos pecunia est. P. Quae quidem non maritata est, yes, if not accompanied with a wife, .—Subst.: mărītāta, ae, f., a wife, a married woman, .—Plur., opp. virgines, viduae, , n. 12.

marmŏrĕus, a, um, adj.
marmor
,

Lit. (class.): signum aëneum, marmoreum, eburneum,: tecta,: solum,a floor,: facere aliquem marmoreum, to make of marble, i. e. as a marble statue, : ponere aliquem marmoreum,: colossus,: villa,.—
Transf.
Of or pertaining to marble, marble- (very rare): ars,.—
Resembling marble (in whiteness or smoothness), marble-like, marble- (mostly poet.): pectus, Lucil. ap. : cervix,: pollex,: palmae,: pedes,: manus,: candor,marblewhiteness,: color,i. e. whiteness,: Paros (from its famous marble quarries),: gelu,. 918: aequor,.—
Adorned with statues: Lucanus in hortis marmoreis,.

la:noun:marmor.html:
marmor, ŏris (also marmur; plur. marmura, Antonius Gripho ap. ; abl. marmori, Corp. Inscr. L. 1012; m., ), n.
root mar-, gleam, glimmer (v. mare), the white or gleaming stone; cf. margarita, = μάρμαρος
,
marble.
Lit.: in omni marmore,: Parium marmor,; : tu secanda marmora Locas,: templum de marmore ponam,; cf.: vivos ducent de marmore vultus,: parietes crusta marmoris operire totius domus,: A MARMORIBVS,one whose office it was to superintend the purchasing and working of marble,: marmora,kinds of marble,; ; ; but blocks or pieces of marble, Hor. l. l.; ; ; ; ; ; v.infra.—
Transf.
Pulverized marble, marble-dust, ; ; ; .—
A marble, i. e.,
A piece of wrought marble, marble statue, etc.: Praxiteles marmore nobilitatus est Gnidiaque Venere,; ; ; : duo marmora,; cf.: lacrimas marmora manant,; so plur., ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
A building of marble, ; .—
In plur., a marble pavement, ; ; Claud. ap. ; .—
A mile-stone of marble: rus marmore tertio notatum,i. e. three miles from town,.—
A marble slab upon a sideboard, .—
A hard, stony tumor in the joints of the horse: plerumque in genibus aut phlegmon oritur, aut marmora,: tumor obduratione convertitur in marmor,.—
Stone in gen., ; : flumen inducit marmora rebus,incrusts,.—
Poet., the bright level surface of the sea; hence, the surface of the sea, the sea in gen.: verrunt extemplo placide mare marmore flavo, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 377 Vahl.); : lento luctantur marmore tonsae,; : Libycum,: spumant vada marmore verso,: marmora pelagi,: infidum,: medium,the surface of a lake,.

la:other:Marica.html:
Mărīca, ae, f.,
a nymph in the territory of Minturnæ, on the river Liris, the fabled mother of the Latins, ; Serv. acc. to , Circe, who was deified after her death. After her was named the lucus Maricae, the grove consecrated to her, ; called also, silva Maricae,; and, querceta Maricae, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 259: palus Maricae,the lake near Minturnæ, where Marius hid himself after his flight from Sylla,.—As subst.: Mărīca, ae, i. e. Minlurnæ, : regna Maricae,the territory of Minturnæ,.

la:other:Mars.html:
Mars (archaic and poet. Māvors, q. v.), Martis (collat. reduplic. form Marmar, in the Song of the Arval Brothers; v. the following, and Mamers), m.
root mar-, gleam; Sanscr. marīkis, beam of light; hence Mars, the bright god; cf.: marmor, mare
,
Mars, who, as father of Romulus, was the primogenitor of the Roman people, the god of war, of husbandry, of shepherds and seers. For him was named the month of Martius, March, the beginning of the Roman year, sqq.: legio Martia ... ab eo deo, a quo populum Romanum generatum accepimus,: Mars pater te precor quaesoque, uti sies volens propitius mihi, etc., ... ut tu morbos visos invisosque viduertatem vastitudinemque, calamitates intemperiasque prohibessis, etc.,; cf., in the Song of the Arval Brothers, NEVE LVERVE MARMAR SINS INCVRRERE IN PLEORIS; for Mars pater, the forms Marspiter, gen. Marspitris, or -tĕris, and Maspiter were also employed,; ; ; Müll.; 9, § 75; 10, § 65; : Mars Gradivus, Quirinus, Silvanus, Ultor, v. under h. vv.: Mars durus,: torvus,: cruentus,: ferus,; : ferox,: bellicus,: fortibus sane oculis Cassius (Martem spirare dicens) se in Siciliam non iturum,. The Salii were destined for his service, ; horses and bulls were offered to him, Paul. ex Müll.; ; : per Martem, a soldier's oath,. He was often appealed to in oaths, etc., esp. by soldiers: Nam neque Duellona mi umquam neque Mars creduat, ni, etc.,; ; .—
Transf.
War, battle, a conflict, engagement, contest, etc.; also the art of war: cum veter occubuit Priamus sub Marte Pelasgo, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 17 Vahl.): Martem accendere cantu,to incite to battle,: apertus,fighting in the open field,: equitem suo alienoque Marte pugnare, i. e. to fight both in their own fashion (on horseback) and in one which was strange to them (on foot), : pugna jam in manus, jam in gladios, ubi Mars est atrocissimus, venerat,: terribili Marte ululare,: captam sine Marte,: quos amisimus cives, eos Martis vis perculit, non ira victoriae,.—Poet.: Mars forensis,a contest in the forum, legal contest,; cf.: et fora Marte suo litigiosa vacent,.—Hence, prov.: suo (nostro, vestro) Marte, by one's own exertions, without the assistance of others: rex ipse suo Marte res suas recuperavit,; : cum vos vestro Marte his rebus omnibus abundetis,.—
The issue of a war or a battle, the fortune of war: cum omnis belli Mars communis, et cum semper incerti exitus proeliorum sint,: communis adhuc Mars belli erat, : aequo Marte,with equal advantage, on equal terms,; ; : pari Marte,: aequato Marte,: verso Marte ( = versā fortunā),: vario Marte pugnatum est,: incerto Marte,: anceps,; : dubius,.—
The planet Mars: Jovis stellae proximum inferiorem orbem tenet πυρόεις, quae stella Martis appellatur, ; ; ; ; : Martis sidus,.—Hence,
Mar-tĭus (Māvortĭus, v.infra), a, um, adj.
Of or belonging to Mars: lupus,sacred to Mars,; cf.: Martius lupus, integer et intactus, gentis nos Martiae et conditoris nostri admonuit, descended from Mars (since Mars is the father of Romulus and Remus), : legio,; : miles,: proles,i. e. Romulus and Remus,: anguis,sacred to Mars,: judicium,i. e. of the Areopagus at Athens, Oud.: Campus; v. campus: harena,a place in the Circus where the gladiators fought,; : gramen,i. e. the Field of Mars,: Martius mensis, the month of March, formerly the first month of the year, : Martii Calendis,: Idus Martiae, the Ides of March, famous as the day on which Julius Cæsar was killed, ; cf. 14, 20, 1 sq.; ; .— In the form Mavortius (poet.): moenia,i. e. Rome,: tellus,i. e. Thrace,: conjux,i. e. Venus,: proles,i. e. the Thebans,; cf.: seges belli (because sprung from the dragon's teeth),.—
Transf.
Warlike, martial: Martia Penthesilea,: Martia saeculi voluptas,: Martius aeris rauci canor,: vulnera,: Thebe,i. e. where many wars were carried on,.—
Of or belonging to the planet Mars: ille fulgor rutilus, horribilisque terris, quem Martium dicitis,.—As subst.: Mar-tĭus, ii, m. (sc. mensis), March, the month of March: Mensium nomina fere aperta sunt, si a Martio, ut antiqui constituerunt, numeres, Nam primus a Marte,.—
Martĭālis, e, adj.
Of or belonging to Mars: Flamen, Varr L. L. 5, § 84 Müll.; 7, § 45 ib.: lupus,sacred to Mars,: ludi,in honor of Mars,: Martialis collis, near the temple of Deus Fidius, Müll.—Subst.: Martĭālis, is, m., a priest of Mars: Martiales quidam Larini appellabantur, ministri publici Martis,.—
Belonging to the legio Martia; hence, Martĭāles, the soldiers of the legio Martia, .

Sanscr. root mar, die; Gr. μαραίνω, μαρασμός; cf. also morbus, morior
,

Transf., to be faint, weak, drooping, feeble, languid, lazy (not in Cic. or Cæs.): annis corpus jam marcet,: marcent luxuria, vino, et epulis per totam hiemem confecti,: otio ac desidia corrupti marcebant,: pavore,; : si marcet animus, si corpus torpet,: amor,: juventa,.—Hence, marcens, entis, P. a., withering, drooping, feeble, wasted away, exhausted, weak, languid, indolent (mostly poet.).
